extracted.intended_audience: students and general readers of American government/history
extracted.subtask_description: Descriptive textbook account of the composition, workings, customs, and constitutional functions of the United States Senate and House of Representatives. Covers chamber layout, membership background, debate styles, election and apportionment rules, and institutional strengths/weaknesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate trains members to improve political efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate so trains its members as to improve their political efficiency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several years of service in a small body, with important and delicate executive work, are worth twice as many years of jostling in the crowd of representatives; if the Senate does not find the man already superior it ought to make him superior. Natural selection also tends to seat the best ability that has flowed into political life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prevailing career experience of senators
rubrics_metrics.description: Many senators have prior legislative or executive experience: a substantial portion had sat in the House of Representatives or in State legislatures, and many had been judges or State governors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples and compiled figures: in the sixty-first Congress 36 of 92 had sat in the House and 39 in State legislatures; in the sixty-second, out of 96 senators, 28 had sat in the House and 39 in State legislatures. Nearly all had held some public function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate chamber layout and public access
rubrics_metrics.description: The chamber is rectangular with a semicircular seating area; the Vice‑President presides from a marble dais; there are great galleries on all four sides (one for the President; others for ladies, diplomatic representatives, the press, and the public); strangers may be brought onto an outer 'floor of the Senate.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Physical features affect proceedings: the room has a slight echo obliging speakers to strain their voices; light enters through glass compartments in the ceiling; few pictures relieve the cold marble tone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Forms of address and seating customs in the Senate
rubrics_metrics.description: A senator always addresses the Chair 'Mr. President,' and refers to other senators by their States (e.g., 'The senator from Ohio').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When two senators rise simultaneously the Chair indicates the one called by his State; Democrats habitually sit on the right of the chair, Republicans on the left, though parties do not face one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nature and purpose of Senate speeches
rubrics_metrics.description: Speeches in the Senate are shorter and less fervid than in the House and are often not made to convince the assembly but to keep a man's opinions before the public and sustain his fame.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The question is usually settled beforehand in committee or a party 'caucus', so many long set discourses on show-days are mere rhetorical thunder addressed to the nation outside and have little bearing on proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Senate social composition and pretensions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Senate contains many men of great wealth and a majority who are or have been lawyers; the commercial element is stronger than formerly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some senators are rich because they are senators; others are senators because they are rich. Senators and their wives are allowed social precedence over members of the House and private citizens; yet the office is temporary and the rank vanishes with it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opportunities for intrigue and misuse of senatorial power
rubrics_metrics.description: There are abundant opportunities for intrigue because important business is done in secrecy of committee rooms or executive session; there are opportunities for misusing senatorial powers, corruption, and blackmail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scandals have arisen (e.g., employing senators as counsel before the Supreme Court where their influence affected appointments). Such men are few but their presence obliges the rest of the Senate to work with them because they hold votes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparative capacities: Senate vs House of Commons
rubrics_metrics.description: Setting the Senate beside the House of Commons, the average natural capacity of its ninety-six members is not above that of the ninety-six best men in the English House.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The House of Commons has more variety of talent and breadth of culture; the Senate excels in legal and business knowledge and practical shrewdness and contains more who could manage business or deliver popular harangues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Constitutional functions of the Senate
rubrics_metrics.description: Three great functions the Fathers intended: (1) securing the rights of the smaller States, (2) advising or controlling the Executive in appointments and treaties, and (3) restraining a single numerous assembly from yielding to sudden and violent passions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The first function is no longer important; the second has produced evils possibly commensurate with its benefits; the third is still discharged and is the basis for the Senate being a moderating power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Stability and tempo of Senate responsiveness
rubrics_metrics.description: Fluctuations of public opinion reach the Senate more slowly owing to its renewal by one-third every second year and longer individual tenure; senators tend to be less democratic in temper and more self-confident.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This slower responsiveness gives continuity in policy and makes the Senate a steadier bulwark against agitation; since 1896 it has been the body to which property and financial powers chiefly look for support.

rubrics_metrics.name: House representation by population and apportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: The House represents the nation on the basis of population; the Constitution provides that 'representatives and direct taxes shall be apportioned among the several States according to their respective numbers.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Congress allots so many members to each State in proportion to its population at the last decennial census; the State determines districts within its area for choosing members.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gerrymandering: aim and techniques
rubrics_metrics.description: The aim of gerrymandering is so to lay out the one-member districts as to secure in the greatest possible number of them a majority for the party which conducts the operation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methods include packing hostile voters into one district or adding friendly voters to marginal districts; historical examples include very long 'shoe-string' districts and 'dumb-bell' shapes used to concentrate particular populations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of at-large representatives when districts are not redrawn
rubrics_metrics.description: When a State legislature has failed to redistribute the State into congressional districts after receiving an increase of representatives, the additional members are elected by the voters of the whole State on a general ticket and are called 'representatives at large.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recent examples cited: Maine elected all its representatives on this plan; Kansas mixed district and general ticket elections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Quorum determination and roll-call customs in the House
rubrics_metrics.description: The quorum of the House is a majority of the whole number. Custom had been to treat as absent all who did not answer on a roll-call, but Speaker Reed asserted the right to count all he saw present and a rule was passed directing him so to count.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The practice was dropped and restored (with two tellers substituting for the Speaker in 1894); this affects whether a House can be treated as organized for business despite roll-call recusals.

rubrics_metrics.name: State variance in electoral franchise for House elections
rubrics_metrics.description: The electoral franchise by which the House is elected is, for each State, the same as that by which the members of the more numerous branch of the State legislature are chosen; franchises varied and States may exclude persons convicted of crime, paupers, illiterates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The fifteenth and fourteenth Amendments constrain but do not fully standardize franchise across States; practical suffrage varies regionally (manhood suffrage prevalent in Northern and Western States).

rubrics_metrics.name: Terms, meeting schedule, and accountability effects for House members
rubrics_metrics.description: Members are elected for two years in even years; the House does not usually meet until a year after election unless the President convokes it sooner, creating intervals where an outgoing House may pass measures contrary to the recently expressed will of the voters.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Debate exists over whether a new Congress should be required to meet sooner (e.g., within six months) to reduce inconveniences of an unorganized, Speakerless elected House.

rubrics_metrics.name: Election expenses and reporting gaps
rubrics_metrics.description: The expense of an election varies greatly and no estimate of the average can be formed because no returns of congressional election expenses are required by law; sometimes expenditures exceed $10,000 in urban districts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Candidates are often aided by local contributions or party funds; official expenses are public. A 1910 statute requires national committees and national congressional campaign committees (and multi-state influencing organizations) to file accounts with the Clerk of the House naming contributors and amounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bribery prevalence and difficulty of contesting elections
rubrics_metrics.description: Although bribery is not rare, comparatively few elections are impeached because proof is difficult and the House—investigating authority—usually meets a year after the election, making investigations protracted and of limited practical effect given two-year terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It was once proposed to transfer trial of election cases to a judicial tribunal because House decisions often follow party lines and investigations would drag on during the member's short term.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demographic and professional composition of House members
rubrics_metrics.description: Most members are between forty and sixty; lawyers constitute roughly two-thirds of members, with next largest groups from manufactures/commerce, agriculture, banking, or journalism; very few are ministers or working men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: College or academic education is common (many emphasize graduation in Directory biographies); residence in Washington and the demands of practice discourage leading lawyers and railway magnates from serving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honorifics and external titles for House members
rubrics_metrics.description: A member of the House enjoys the title of 'Honourable,' given not merely within the House but in the world at large.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Share of the title with state senators, higher officials, and judges reduces its social distinctiveness.

rubrics_metrics.name: House lacks executive confirmation functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The House has no share in the executive functions of the Senate and nothing to do with confirming appointments or approving treaties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This institutional separation defines different powers and responsibilities between the two chambers.
